games.title: RuneScape: Dragonwilds
games.blurb: Co-operative survival crafting on the dragon-haunted continent of Ashenfall.
games.deck: Jagex’s survival spinoff leaves Early Access and becomes the first RuneScape game on console, magic and all.
body: On the forgotten continent of Ashenfall, dragons have awoken. RuneScape: Dragonwilds asks you to gather, build, skill and craft your way toward the Dragon Queen, alone or with up to three friends, and its 1.0 launch is the first time a RuneScape game has shipped on console, with crossplay.

As of GameDaily’s Sept 19 roundup, neither Metacritic nor OpenCritic had enough reviews for an aggregate, with individual critic marks ranging from 65 to 90, so we show a single outlet score instead. The Outerhaven (4/5, played on Series X) calls it an entertaining survival RPG that gives the franchise a new identity. It singles out the skill system (levelling through use), magic that’s useful both in and out of combat, and flexible building that works well on a controller.

Gfinity’s 1.0 review is a useful counterweight: breathtaking visuals and a highly rewarding magic system (“the magic system gives it its own flair to stand out”), undercut by vague tutorial quests, punishing enemy aggression and a stingy stamina bar that make solo play overwhelming. Both reviews agree the game is at its best with friends.

One caution: shortly after launch, console players reported corrupted world saves. Jagex acknowledged the issue and said the team was working flat-out to resolve it. Check the latest patch notes before you sink in the hours.

quote.text: The magic system gives it its own flair to stand out.

pros: Strong co-op for 1–4 players with crossplay
cons: Launch reports of console save corruption
games.playIf: you’ve got a crew ready for Valheim-style co-op and a soft spot for Gielinor.

hltb.note: Small sample (7 / 6 / 1 players polled), largely from Early Access builds.

seriesX.text: Targets 60fps and generally feels responsive, with brief drops in busy areas or around elaborate settlements and some texture pop-in when travelling fast.

pc.text: Gfinity reports it ran smoothly with no frame drops on an ASUS TUF Gaming A15 laptop.

other.text: Console save corruption was reported after launch. Jagex acknowledged it (as of Sept 19).

a11y.text: Settings for subtitles, audio, camera behaviour and controller sensitivity, plus custom world options to adjust hunger and thirst. The Outerhaven notes that some small text and icons are hard to read from a distance.

nowOrWait.text: The co-op fun is real, but check that the console save-corruption fix has landed before you commit a long-term world.

games.title: Kernel Hearts
games.blurb: Magical-girl action roguelite with optional four-player co-op.
games.deck: Android magical girls climb the Tower of Babel to punch out angels — and, eventually, God.
body: The debut from Buenos Aires studio Ephemera Games has one of the year’s wildest pitches: the M.A.H.O.U. Unit, cybernetic magical girls, climbs the Tower of Babel through biblical monsters to settle things with God directly. Runs mix hack-and-slash combos, temporary powers and a flashy transformation, while a 256KB MAHOU.OS chip system handles permanent builds. Up to four players can climb together online.

We couldn’t find an OpenCritic or Metacritic aggregate at press time, so here’s what individual critics say. Game Critix (4.5/5) called it “gloriously bonkers,” praising fast, responsive combat and co-op that feels designed in rather than bolted on, though big fights can get hard to read.

NoobFeed, around two dozen hours in, found open arena maps rather than rooms, a “sin meter” that summons a Sky Angel if you linger too long, and bosses that are the highlight. On-screen combo guides and a forgiving dodge make it approachable. On the other hand, it found the combat simple and repetitive, the characters other than Fernet thin, and early meta-progression slow, and it flagged a sharp difficulty spike from the third level.
A full run can take up to two hours, which NoobFeed notes is long for the genre, and the finale lands better than you’d expect.
pros: Fast combat with on-screen combo guides
cons: Combat can feel simple and repetitive
games.playIf: you want Hades-style runs with loud anime flair and a squad of friends in the party.

hltb.note: HowLongToBeat lists the game but no completion times yet. NoobFeed notes a single full run can take up to two hours.

pc.text: No frame-rate data yet. On PC, NoobFeed reports private and public co-op lobbies ran well, but warns latency is a risk for combos and perfect dodges online.

a11y.text: Three difficulty modes (Story, Normal, Sinner) that you can switch on the fly, plus a HUD showing available combos as you input them. On PC at review time, NoobFeed reported movement locked to WASD with no remapping. A full accessibility breakdown is not yet reported.

nowOrWait.text: It’s day one on Ultimate and PC Game Pass and at its best in co-op. Solo players could wait for balance patches to the early meta-progression.

games.title: Ninja Gaiden 4
games.dev: PlatinumGames & Team Ninja / Xbox Game Studios
games.blurb: The hack-and-slash series returns with brutal, high-speed combat.
games.deck: Team Ninja and PlatinumGames’ blood-soaked revival slices its way into Game Pass Premium.

aggregate.label: OpenCritic Top Critic Average
aggregate.note: Originally released October 2025; reviews reflect that launch.

body: Already on Ultimate and PC Game Pass since its October 2025 launch, Ninja Gaiden 4 now joins the Premium tier — and if you skipped it the first time, this is your cue. Team Ninja and PlatinumGames share the sword, with newcomer Yakumo leading and Ryu Hayabusa cast as his rival.

The critical story is simple: the combat is phenomenal and everything around it is merely fine. It holds an 82 Top Critic Average on OpenCritic. IGN (8/10) said that despite a disappointing story and bland level design, the excellent combat makes it “one of the best 3D action games in recent memory.” GamesRadar+ gave it a perfect 5/5, TheGamer (4.5/5) said Platinum clearly understands what makes the series special, and GameSpot (8/10) said it brings the series back with a bang.

Not everyone was sold on the extras. PC Gamer (69/100) felt the bloody good combat carries it through its more extraneous “modern” additions, and Hardcore Gamer landed at 3.5/5. OpenCritic’s critic consensus sums it up: linear levels and a simple story hold it back slightly, but the core loop and intense battles make it a standout.

A note for newcomers: the easiest setting, Hero mode, comes with automated assists — but Can I Play That? strongly criticised how the game penalises players who turn them on (see Accessibility below).

quote.text: One of the best 3D action games in recent memory.

pros: Relentless pace from start to finish
cons: Assists lock you into the easiest difficulty
games.playIf: you judge a game by how good it feels to dash, parry and dismember — story strictly optional.

facts.v: PlatinumGames & Team Ninja / Xbox Game Studios

seriesX.text: 30, 60 and 120fps options that hit their targets fairly consistently. Digital Foundry recommends the 60fps mode as largely stable and smooth.

seriesS.text: No 120fps mode. The 60fps mode targets a low native 720p with dynamic resolution, very blurry textures and effects such as SSR, AO and motion blur disabled. Digital Foundry compared the look to a “PS3 era game”. The 30fps mode has a variable, unlocked frame rate.

pc.text: Digital Foundry’s review headline: “Platinum’s bespoke engine shines — especially on PC, PS5 Pro.”

a11y.text: Can I Play That? praises customisable HUD colours and text sizes, high-contrast options and legible subtitles, and notes assists including Auto Assist, Auto Block, Auto Heal, Auto Movement and Auto Interact. But controls aren’t fully remappable, turning on Auto Assist, Auto Block or Auto Heal forces the easiest (“Hero”) difficulty, and Auto Movement disables scoring. The reviewer called its handling of accessibility the worst he has seen.

nowOrWait.text: It’s been out for a year, it’s polished, and it’s now in Premium. Series S players should expect a big visual downgrade.

games.title: Dune: Awakening
games.blurb: Single and multiplayer open-world survival on Arrakis.
games.deck: Funcom’s Arrakis survival epic finally lands on Xbox — with a full solo mode, optional PvP and a finished Book One story.

aggregate.label: OpenCritic Top Critic Average
aggregate.note: Mostly reflects the June 2025 PC launch. Checked Sept 28, 2026 (an earlier snapshot read 81).

body: Fifteen months after its PC debut, Dune: Awakening arrives on Xbox Series X|S with Update 1.5 — per Gamersuniverse, the biggest patch the game has ever received. Funcom’s own launch post on Xbox Wire lays out what changed: a full single-player mode with three difficulty presets (or every setting customisable, from sandstorms to XP multipliers and durability), the conclusion of Book One so the whole story can be played start to finish, and a promise that every part of the game can now be played entirely in PvE.

The core loop is survival pressure at its purest. You distill water, chase shade, piece together a base and dash across open sand before a worm erases your afternoon. Critics have been consistently warm: it holds an 80 Top Critic Average on OpenCritic. Eurogamer (4/5) marvelled that it juggles harsh survival, RPG and open-world PvP — “Somehow, it pulls it off.” IGN (8/10) called it an excellent survival MMO that brilliantly captures life on Arrakis, while GameSpot (7/10) felt it stumbles in the endgame and GamesRadar+ (3/5) found irritations and bloat holding it back.

Funcom says the endgame has been rebuilt since then: the Landsraad faction war is now mission-driven and works in single-player, late-game items need fewer rare materials, and a new Specializations system lets you invest in crafting, gathering, exploration, combat and sabotage. Combat got a pass too, with a wider parry window and improved enemy AI.

Xbox-specific coverage is upbeat about going solo. Complete Xbox says the new mode makes the game far easier to recommend to players who avoid multiplayer survival, and But Why Tho argues it’s simply a great survival game, alone or with others. The caveats are technical: MKAU Gaming and But Why Tho both report textures streaming in late on Series X, and MKAU also flags cutscene flicker and a map that’s too restricted when zooming.
pros: Arrakis is brutal and hugely atmospheric
Full solo mode, private servers and optional PvP
Deep crafting and a rebuilt endgame
cons: Launch flicker and texture pop reported on Series X
Menus and map feel clunky on a controller
Endgame criticised in the original reviews
games.playIf: you want a survival sandbox with real stakes — and have always wanted to outrun a sandworm on your own terms.

hltb.note: HowLongToBeat marks it “Multiplayer Focused”, and these samples are tiny, mostly from PC.

seriesX.text: Two modes: Performance (60fps, dynamic 4K) and Quality (30fps, dynamic 4K); Series X renders at a higher native resolution with enhanced visuals. iXBT reports it mostly holds 60fps with occasional dips to around 54. Reviewers flagged cutscene flicker and slow texture streaming at launch.

seriesS.text: Performance mode runs at a lower dynamic resolution (roughly 720p–1080p) to hold 60fps; iXBT, citing the Xbox Nation channel, reports drops are almost imperceptible.

pc.text: Gamersuniverse says a year of patches has dramatically improved server stability on PC, and the console work brought Nanite foliage and more efficient sandstorm rendering to PC too.

a11y.text: Single-player offers three difficulty presets or full customisation of gameplay settings (sandstorms, harvesting and XP multipliers, building limits, durability and more). PvP is entirely optional. A detailed accessibility-menu breakdown (subtitles, remapping, colour options) is not yet reported for the Xbox version.

nowOrWait.text: The solo mode and a full Book One make this the best version yet. Expect some launch-week visual rough edges on Series X.

games.title: Well Dweller
games.blurb: A dark fairy-tale metroidvania starring a tiny bird with a matchstick.
games.deck: A one-developer dark fairy tale that just became one of 2026’s best-reviewed games — and it’s day one on Game Pass.

aggregate.label: OpenCritic Top Critic Average
aggregate.note: Push Square also reported a Metacritic 91 (PC) at launch.

body: Solo developer Kyle Thompson (Crypt Custodian, Islets) has quietly dropped one of the year’s best-reviewed games straight into Game Pass. You play Glimmer, the eldest in a family of birds hiding at the bottom of a well. A queen obsessed with feathered gowns has hunted birds nearly to extinction, and when her hunter carries off your family, a matchstick becomes your sword, your health bar (the flame dims as you take hits) and, later, a slingshot-fired springboard for traversal.

Critics are close to unanimous: a 90 Top Critic Average on OpenCritic with 100% recommending it. Screen Rant (9/10) said it “might be one of 2026's best sleeper hits,” and Worth Playing (9/10) praised “a polished take on the genre.” NoobFeed notes the Hollow Knight influence is obvious early on, but says the game earns its own identity through tight combat, clever traversal and a moody storybook world. It singles out Eric Thompson’s synthy soundtrack and one of the best maps in the genre, with free fast travel that unlocks early.

Combat is simple and dependable: a two-hit combo, a homing flaming bottle you swat at enemies, invincible slides and a timing-based heal that briefly boosts your attack. Trinkets work like Hollow Knight’s charms, and across 15 biomes you pick up bubble jumps, wall climbs, wind riding and the slingshot.

The knocks are small. Screen Rant found the platforming slightly slippery; NoobFeed wanted tougher bosses and one more combat idea, and felt that buying trinket slots cheaply undercuts exploring for them. For about $20, it’s an easy recommendation — and on Ultimate or PC Game Pass it costs nothing extra.

quote.text: Might be one of 2026's best sleeper hits.

pros: Superb map and free fast travel
cons: The combat loop could use more variety
games.playIf: Hollow Knight hooked you but you’d welcome a gentler, funnier, more compact adventure.

hltb.note: Early, small sample (9 / 6 / 28 players polled). NoobFeed estimates 10–14 hours for a regular playthrough.

other.text: On PS5, NoobFeed reports it runs smoothly overall, with only a slight delay when moving between screens.

a11y.text: Three difficulty levels (Easy, Normal, Hard) plus accessibility options that make it more forgiving still, according to NoobFeed. You don’t lose currency on death. A full options breakdown is not yet reported.

nowOrWait.text: It launched polished, it’s short, and it’s free with Ultimate or PC Game Pass. No reason to wait.

games.title: Mad King Redemption
games.blurb: Pixel-art 2.5D beat ’em up with roguelite progression.
games.deck: An Early Access 2.5D beat ’em up with a roguelite heart and a very bad king.
body: A desperate king tries to raise his dead queen with forbidden magic, loses his mind and takes the kingdom with him. Mad King Redemption sends four heroes, each with their own fighting style, stats and backstory, through randomised runs that blend classic brawling with 2.5D platforming. It has been in Early Access on Steam since May 14, reached the Xbox Store in August, and joined Game Pass on Sept 23. Treat it as a work in progress.

There’s no aggregate score, but Gaming Cypher’s Early Access review (8.5/10) liked what it saw: detailed pixel-art sprites under dynamic 3D lighting, a Hades II-style Brotherhood Camp hub for permanent upgrades, and a heroes roster ranging from Branok the Wrestler’s crowd control to Elowen the Sorcerer’s ranged spells and healing.
The standout mechanic is risk and reward: lean on the Mad King’s forbidden powers and your Corruption meter fills, leading to an overcharged frenzy followed by an instant 50% health penalty.

The rough edges are real, though. Gaming Cypher reports depth-perception problems in the 2.5D view, where swings and airborne hitboxes don’t line up, cheap chip damage from some shielded enemies, and a restrictive stamina meter. Its conclusion: iron out the jank and this has “all the makings of an indie brawler classic.”

quote.text: All the makings of an indie brawler classic.

games.playIf: you love arcade brawlers and don’t mind getting in early.

trailer.title: Mad King Redemption XBOX Game Pass Announcement trailer

hltb.note: HowLongToBeat lists the game with no completion times yet.

nowOrWait.text: It’s on Game Pass, so a few runs cost nothing extra. Wait for the full release if hitbox jank bothers you.

games.title: Minecraft Dungeons II
games.dev: Mojang Studios & Double Eleven / Xbox Game Studios
games.blurb: Dungeon-crawling sequel with an interconnected world and a new dimension, the Sift.
games.deck: Mojang’s dungeon-crawler sequel opens up the world. It launches tomorrow, day one on Game Pass, and the first reviews landed this morning.
body: Reviews went live on the morning of Sept 28, the day before launch, so there’s no aggregate score yet and we show the first individual verdicts instead. The sequel swaps the first game’s mission select for an interconnected world, adds a jump (which brings verticality and even parkour), splits armor into four slots and introduces the Sift, which GamingBolt’s preview called Minecraft’s first new dimension in more than 14 years.

IGN (6/10) found a brief, shallow ARPG: a roughly seven-hour story, samey hack-and-slash and a thin endgame (Soul Storms) for now. It welcomes the jump, more customisable gear and the Sift, “one of the few ways in which it branches out,” and concludes it’s a fine way to spend a mindless night or two with friends. Its subhead: “This shallow sequel provides some peaceful button mashing, but does little to stand out.”

GamingBolt, playing on PC, rated it “Average”. It praised the good looks, environmental variety, decent combat and solid optimisation, but criticised stingy Unique drops, crafting reduced to upgrades and rerolls, a single timed endgame activity, no stash or dungeon overlay map, and features missing from the original.

The previews were warmer. GamesRadar+ called it “a real breath of fresh air” for its pick-up-and-play simplicity, and PCGamesN said it smartly fills a gap as a more casual dungeon crawler. Mojang has said more endgame content is planned after launch, and the first paid DLC is due later this year.

quote.text: This shallow sequel provides some peaceful button mashing, but does little to stand out.

pros: The Sift is a vivid new dimension
Friendly for younger and co-op players
cons: Areas held back for paid DLC (GamingBolt)
games.playIf: you want a low-stakes, drop-in dungeon crawler for family co-op nights and don’t need deep buildcraft.

trailer.title: MINECRAFT DUNGEONS II | Official Gameplay Trailer

facts.v: Mojang Studios & Double Eleven / Xbox Game Studios

hltb.note: No HowLongToBeat data yet (it launches Sept 29). Reviewers’ story length varies: IGN puts it at roughly seven hours, while GamingBolt took 25 hours to beat the story.

pc.text: GamingBolt says it ran very well at 1440p with most settings on Ultra and DLSS set to Quality, with no performance issues.

a11y.text: Not yet reported. Xbox Wire notes a hold-to-open mini inventory designed so couch co-op players can each swap gear on screen simultaneously.

nowOrWait.text: Early reviews are mixed-to-middling. It’s included with Ultimate and PC Game Pass, so try it for a co-op night rather than buying it outright.

games.title: Keeper
games.blurb: A wordless adventure about an awakened lighthouse and a seabird.
games.deck: Double Fine’s wordless walking-lighthouse odyssey is as strange and gorgeous as it sounds.

aggregate.label: OpenCritic Top Critic Average
aggregate.note: Originally released October 2025; reviews reflect that launch.

body: A long-forgotten lighthouse wakes up, befriends a spirited seabird and strides off into realms beyond understanding. That’s Keeper, Double Fine’s story told entirely without words, which arrives in Game Pass Premium on Friday, October 2, after launching on Ultimate and PC Game Pass in October 2025.

It sits on an 81 Top Critic Average, but the spread is the story. Eurogamer awarded 5/5, and IGN (9/10) called exploring its surreal world “a feast for the senses.” PC Gamer (90/100) praised its tightly designed puzzles and cerebral platforming, and GameSpot (9/10) called it Double Fine “at its most confident.”

Pure Xbox (8/10), which reviewed it on Series X and ROG Xbox Ally, describes very casual, cosy puzzles built to eliminate frustration, with the camera subtly guiding you forward. It warns that the first half can feel paint-by-numbers but says the second half changes things up with ambitious sequences that “elevate” the game. Its advice: stick with it at least until the midpoint.

The dissenters aim at the game beneath the art. Game Rant (6/10) found it absolutely gorgeous but possibly the blandest entry in Double Fine’s catalogue to play, and Game Informer (7.5/10) said it fares far better as a piece of art than as a game. OpenCritic’s consensus lands on gorgeous visuals, a genuinely original feel and uneven early pacing.
pros: Strong second half and heartfelt wordless story
games.playIf: you want a strange, beautiful trip more than a mechanical workout.

facts.v: Double Fine Productions / Xbox Game Studios

seriesX.text: Pure Xbox reports the frame rate jumps between 30fps and 60fps depending on the situation. It still preferred Series X over ROG Xbox Ally for the visuals.

pc.text: DSOGaming’s headline: Keeper runs at 60fps in native 4K only on Medium settings with an NVIDIA RTX 5090, so it’s demanding at the high end.

a11y.text: Per Double Fine: multiple volume controls and mono sound; playable without rapid button presses; basic input remapping (everything except Pause and Interaction), plus switch-aim sensitivity; screen narration for game and menu navigation; text size and weight options; interaction-prompt frequency; colour alternatives; and a High Contrast Mode added in a post-launch update.

src.label: Can I Play That? (high contrast update)

nowOrWait.text: It’s about five hours, fully patched, and in Premium from October 2. Premium members can start Friday; Ultimate and PC Game Pass members can play today.
